examples.solution_text:
(a) The line joins the centre to the circumference. It is a radius.
(b) The line joins two points on the circumference and passes through the centre. It is a diameter.
(c) The line joins two points on the circumference but misses the centre. It is a chord.
(d) A diameter joins two points on the circumference, so it is a special chord.
(e) The whole curve is the circumference. A part of it is an arc.
(f) It is a tangent.

(a) Two radii and an arc form the boundary. The region is a sector.
(b) A chord and an arc form the boundary, so the region is a segment. It is the larger region made by the chord, so it is the major segment. The smaller unshaded region is the minor segment.

(a) The diameter divides the circle into two equal halves. The shaded half is a semicircle.
(b) The two radii meet at a right angle. The shaded quarter is a quadrant.
$K$ is the centre: points on the circumference are an equal distance from it.

methods.description: Identify radius, diameter, chord or tangent by checking endpoints, passage through the centre and contact with the circumference; apply the same definitions to descriptions and labelled figures.

methods.description: Distinguish a sector bounded by two radii and an arc from a segment bounded by a chord and an arc; identify major and minor segments by comparing the two regions.

methods.description: Identify a semicircle from a diameter and half-circle region, and a quadrant from two perpendicular radii and a quarter-circle region.

methods.description: Identify the centre as the point an equal distance from every point on the circumference.

examples.derivation: A, B and C have coordinates (1.6 cos θ, 1.6 sin θ) for θ = 25°, 145° and 265°. Each is therefore 1.6 units from K = (0,0), which is also the drawn circle's centre. Identifying K as the centre follows the equal-distance definition taught at source lines 154–163. No numerical calculation is required in the student solution.
